assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Molecule
items.clue: A group of atoms bonded together.

items.label: Element
items.clue: A substance made of only one type of atom.

items.label: Rate of reaction
items.clue: How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed.

items.label: Exothermic reaction
items.clue: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter.

questions.stem: Which statement about atoms and elements is correct?

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 types of atom occur naturally.
Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 substances exist in total.
Matter is made of atoms, and every element in the table is natural.
Matter is made of atoms, with one type of atom per compound.

questions.explanation: Matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms, and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, which are the elements.

questions.stem: There are only about 100 naturally occurring types of atom, yet chemists have identified millions of different substances. How is this possible?

options.text: Millions of other types of atom are still waiting to be discovered.
Those atoms can join in many different ratios and arrangements.
Atoms change into atoms of new elements when substances react.
Every new compound must contain its own new type of atom.

questions.explanation: A limited set of atom types gives an unlimited set of compounds, because atoms can combine in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?

options.text: Properties change smoothly from the first element to the last one.
Only physical properties such as melting point follow a pattern.
Similar properties recur at regular intervals across the table.
Elements sharing a period have very similar properties.

questions.explanation: Periodic means repeating: as the elements are listed in order, similar chemical and physical properties reappear at regular intervals.

questions.stem: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react vigorously with water in a similar way. Which feature of their atomic structure explains this?

options.text: Their atoms all contain the same total number of electrons.
Their atoms all have the same number of occupied shells.
Their electrons fill the same number of energy levels.
Each atom has just one electron in its outer shell.

questions.explanation: Li is 2,1; Na is 2,8,1; K is 2,8,8,1. Each has a single outer electron to lose, so each reacts in the same way, which is why they share a group.

questions.stem: According to the key ideas, in what ways can atoms bond to one another?

options.text: By sharing electrons, or by fusing the two nuclei firmly together.
By transferring electrons from one atom to another, or by sharing them.
By transferring protons between atoms, or by sharing protons.
By sharing electrons only, since transfer is not bonding.

questions.explanation: Atoms bond either by transferring electrons from one atom to another, which gives ions, or by sharing electrons, which gives covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Magnesium burns in oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. What happens to electrons as this compound forms?

options.text: Each magnesium atom shares its two electrons with an oxygen atom.
Each oxygen atom transfers two electrons to a magnesium atom.
Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to an oxygen atom.
Each magnesium atom gives two protons to an oxygen atom.

questions.explanation: Magnesium has two outer electrons to lose and oxygen needs two to fill its outer shell, giving Mg2+ and O2- ions in MgO.

questions.stem: Why do the key ideas say that the shapes of molecules and the arrangement of giant structures are of great importance?

options.text: Because the shape of a substance decides only how it looks to us.
Because two substances made of the same atoms always behave alike.
Because a giant structure is really just a very big molecule.
Because how the particles are arranged decides how they behave.

questions.explanation: Structure is a cause, not a picture: how atoms are bonded and arranged controls properties such as hardness, melting point and conductivity.

questions.stem: Diamond and graphite are both giant structures containing only carbon atoms, yet graphite is soft and conducts electricity while diamond is hard and does not. Why?

options.text: The carbon atoms are bonded in different arrangements.
Graphite holds a small amount of metal that carries the current.
Graphite contains a softer type of carbon atom than diamond does.
Graphite is a molecule, so it is not a giant structure.

questions.explanation: Same atoms, different structure: graphite forms layers with delocalised electrons, while diamond is a rigid three-dimensional network.

questions.stem: The key ideas state that there are barriers to reaction. What does this mean?

options.text: Reacting particles are kept apart by a physical layer between them.
Substances have to be melted before their particles can react.
Colliding particles need a minimum amount of energy before they react.
Every collision between particles will produce a reaction.

questions.explanation: The barrier is an energy requirement. Collisions below that energy do not lead to reaction, so different barriers give different rates.

questions.stem: Two different reactions are carried out at the same temperature and concentration, but one goes much more slowly than the other. What best explains the difference?

options.text: A physical barrier keeps its particles apart in the flask.
The slower reaction releases less energy overall than the faster.
Its particles are colliding much less often than the other.
The slower reaction has the higher energy barrier to overcome.

questions.explanation: A higher barrier means a smaller fraction of collisions carry enough energy to react, so fewer collisions succeed and the rate is lower.

questions.stem: The key ideas state that chemical reactions take place in only three different ways. What are those three ways?

options.text: Proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing.
Proton transfer, neutron transfer and electron transfer only.
Proton sharing, neutron sharing and electron transfer only.
Electron transfer, energy transfer and proton sharing.

questions.explanation: These are exactly the three ways given in the specification, covering acid reactions, redox reactions and the formation of covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution. In terms of the three ways reactions take place, what happens here?

options.text: An electron is transferred from the acid to the hydroxide ions.
A proton is transferred from the acid to the alkali.
A proton is transferred from the alkali across to the acid.
The two solutions only mix and dilute one another here.

questions.explanation: The acid donates H+, which is simply a proton, to the OH- ions from the alkali, forming water. This is proton transfer.
